# Cluster, gradient or artefact {#sec-b14}



::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** When does a figure become a testable subtype hypothesis?\
**For:** translational researchers, doctoral students and reviewers who meet cluster maps of patients ·
**Prerequisites:** denominators and units (@sec-b03), the person as independent unit (@sec-b13), basic idea of
distances between observations\
**In the course:** [W5 · Causality, trajectories and phenotypes](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) ·
**Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b14-case}

A fictitious trauma research group has six routine values from the first day after major trauma in 300 people:
C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, lactate, leukocytes, platelets and body temperature. A colleague shows a
two-dimensional map in which the patients form three islands. The proposal is to call them "hyperinflammatory",
"intermediate" and "quiet" subtypes, to name them in the manuscript and to stratify a planned trial by subtype. The
group leader has to decide whether the word "subtype" goes into the manuscript and the trial protocol. The data in this
chapter are *synthetic* and were generated, on purpose, from a single continuous severity gradient without any
groups. The task is to find out which analysis would have revealed that – and what evidence would be needed before a
subtype label may change what happens to a patient.

## Core reading {#sec-b14-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended for W5 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::



**What the table contains.** One row per person, six columns with six units: mg/L, pg/mL, mmol/L, 10^9^/L twice and
°C. The independent unit is the person; n = 300. Any clustering method needs a distance between two people, and that
distance depends on how the six columns are put on a common scale. Without scaling, platelets (standard deviation
59 × 10^9^/L) and interleukin-6 (61 pg/mL) dominate, while lactate
(0.8 mmol/L) and temperature (0.5 °C) hardly count. After
standardisation to z-scores, each marker counts equally. After a log transformation of the skewed markers, the
distances change again. Scaling is a modelling decision with clinical content, not a technical preliminary. In the lab, k-means on the
original units agrees with the z-score solution only with an adjusted Rand index of 0.37
(1 means identical partitions, 0 chance agreement): changing the units reassigns a large share of the patients.

**A gradient cut into slices.** A principal component analysis (PCA) of the z-scores shows one dominant axis: the first
component carries 62.5% of the variance and correlates at 0.93 with
the hidden severity used to generate the data. k-means clustering with three clusters [@hartigan1979kmeans] does what
it is built to do: it minimises the sum of squared distances between each person and the nearest of three centres. On a gradient, it
returns three slices (@fig-b14-slices). The left panel looks like three groups because the colours say so. The right
panel shows the decisive detail: the cluster boundaries do not sit in empty regions. They cut through the densest part
of the distribution.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![k-means with k = 3 on z-scored markers (*synthetic*, n = 300 persons). (a) First two principal components, colour and shape by cluster. (b) Distribution of the first principal component, stacked by cluster: the clusters are adjacent slices without gaps between them.](b14-cluster-gradient-artefact_files/figure-epub/fig-b14-slices-1.png){#fig-b14-slices fig-alt='Two panels. Panel a is a scatter plot of the first against the second principal component; three clusters, shown with different colours and point shapes, lie side by side along the horizontal axis without visible gaps. Panel b is a histogram of the first principal component with bars stacked by cluster; the histogram has a single broad peak, and the cluster boundaries fall on its flanks and near its centre rather than in a trough.'}
:::
:::


**Methods that agree for the wrong reason.** Three further analyses seem to confirm the islands. A Gaussian mixture
model (**mclust**, @scrucca2016mclust) selects 6 components by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) on
z-scores and 3 on log-transformed markers. BIC counts how many bell-shaped components are needed to
describe the shape of the cloud; a skewed or curved cloud needs several, even without groups. Bootstrap stability
looks reassuring as well: when the 300 persons are resampled and re-clustered a hundred times, the three clusters are
recovered with mean Jaccard similarities between 0.77 and
0.91 [@hennig2007stability]. By the usual guidance for this measure, values above 0.75
count as stable [@hennig2026fpc]. Stability, however, shows that the same cut is made each time, not that there is a
seam to cut along. A knife set at the same place gives reproducible slices of a loaf.

**The question behind the question.** Every clustering algorithm returns as many groups as it is asked for. Asking
"how many clusters are there?" therefore presupposes that there are clusters. The first question is a different one:
is there any discontinuity in the population, or do the patients vary along one or a few continuous axes? Only if the
answer is the former does the choice of k become meaningful.

**What would distinguish groups from a gradient.** A real group structure leaves a trough in the density between
groups. A simple diagnostic compares the density of the first component at the boundary between two k-means clusters
with the density at the two cluster centres. Here, the ratio is 1.18: the boundary lies
where people are *more* frequent than at the centres. The counter-check (@sec-b14-countercheck) builds a data set with
a real gap and shows how this ratio falls.

**UMAP islands.** Two-dimensional maps such as UMAP [@mcinnes2018umap] are built to keep each person's nearest
neighbours close. The documentation of the reference implementation states that UMAP, like t-SNE, does not completely
preserve density and can create false tears in clusters, yielding a finer clustering than is present in the data
[@umaplearn2026docs].
Island sizes, gaps and distances between islands are not measurements; @chari2023specious show how strongly such
maps can distort the structure of single-cell data. A map is a reason to look, not evidence of subtypes.

**The baseline.** The biometrically sensible baseline for a gradient is a continuous score, here the first principal
component. In the lab, a model for a *synthetic* day-7 organ dysfunction outcome fits better with the continuous score
(AIC 326.0) than with the three cluster labels (AIC 337.1). Cutting the
gradient into slices throws information away. A label also hides similarity: two patients who lie just either side
of a boundary receive different names, while two patients at opposite ends of the same slice share one.

**The most important assumption.** **A cluster label claims a discontinuity in the population. It is supported only if
a gap survives changes of scaling, algorithm and sample, reappears in an independent cohort and the label adds
information beyond a continuous score.** Without this, "three subtypes" describes the analysis, not the patients.

**Question for the workshop.** Which observation would convince you that the three islands are subtypes rather than
slices: the same islands after log transformation, a trough in the density, reproduction in another centre or a
different treatment effect in a randomised trial? Rank the four and justify the order.

## Lab {#sec-b14-lab}

The lab needs **mclust**, **cluster**, **ggplot2** and **patchwork** and runs in a few seconds.

### Step 1: simulate a gradient without groups

All values are *synthetic assumptions*. A single latent severity score drives all six markers; three of them are
right-skewed, as many inflammatory markers are. The day-7 outcome depends on the same score, continuously.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1414)                                    # same data each time this chunk runs
n <- 300
make_markers <- function(severity) {              # one latent score drives all six markers
  m <- length(severity)
  data.frame(
    crp_mg_l          = pmax(1, 60 + 35 * severity + rnorm(m, 0, 20)),
    il6_pg_ml         = exp(3.6 + 0.8 * severity + rnorm(m, 0, 0.45)),
    lactate_mmol_l    = exp(log(1.8) + 0.30 * severity + rnorm(m, 0, 0.25)),
    leukocytes_10e9_l = pmax(1, 11 + 2.5 * severity + rnorm(m, 0, 2.5)),
    platelets_10e9_l  = pmax(20, 220 - 35 * severity + rnorm(m, 0, 45)),
    temperature_c     = 37.4 + 0.4 * severity + rnorm(m, 0, 0.35))
}
severity <- rnorm(n)                              # continuous, unimodal: no subtypes by construction
markers <- make_markers(severity)
organ_dysfunction <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.2 + 1.3 * severity))   # synthetic day-7 outcome
round(sapply(markers, function(x) c(median = median(x), sd = sd(x))), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>        crp_mg_l il6_pg_ml lactate_mmol_l leukocytes_10e9_l platelets_10e9_l
#> median    62.95     38.73           1.81             10.94           213.73
#> sd        39.66     61.02           0.84              3.56            59.02
#>        temperature_c
#> median         37.46
#> sd              0.53
```


:::
:::


### Step 2: three scalings and a PCA


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
log_vars <- c("crp_mg_l", "il6_pg_ml", "lactate_mmol_l")
x_raw <- as.matrix(markers)                       # original units
x_z <- scale(markers)                             # z-scores: every marker counts equally
markers_log <- markers
markers_log[log_vars] <- lapply(markers_log[log_vars], log)
x_logz <- scale(markers_log)                      # log for skewed markers, then z-scores
pca <- prcomp(x_z)
pc1_share <- summary(pca)$importance["Proportion of Variance", "PC1"]
cor_pc1 <- cor(pca$x[, 1], severity)
round(summary(pca)$importance[, 1:3], 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                          PC1   PC2   PC3
#> Standard deviation     1.936 0.773 0.702
#> Proportion of Variance 0.625 0.100 0.082
#> Cumulative Proportion  0.625 0.724 0.806
```


:::
:::


### Step 3: k-means with two to five clusters

The mean silhouette width compares, for every person, the distance to the own cluster with the distance to the
nearest other cluster [@rousseeuw1987silhouette]; values near 1 indicate well-separated clusters.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(cluster)
library(mclust)
set.seed(14141)
d_z <- dist(x_z)
km <- lapply(2:5, function(k) kmeans(x_z, centers = k, nstart = 25))
silhouette_mean <- sapply(km, function(m) mean(silhouette(m$cluster, d_z)[, "sil_width"]))
names(silhouette_mean) <- paste0("k=", 2:5)
cluster_ref <- km[[2]]$cluster                    # reference solution: z-scores, k = 3
cluster_raw <- kmeans(x_raw, centers = 3, nstart = 25)$cluster
cluster_log <- kmeans(x_logz, centers = 3, nstart = 25)$cluster
ari_raw <- adjustedRandIndex(cluster_ref, cluster_raw)   # 1 = identical partition, 0 = chance agreement
ari_log <- adjustedRandIndex(cluster_ref, cluster_log)
round(c(silhouette_mean, ARI_raw_vs_z = ari_raw, ARI_log_vs_z = ari_log), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>          k=2          k=3          k=4          k=5 ARI_raw_vs_z ARI_log_vs_z 
#>        0.335        0.247        0.233        0.192        0.368        0.464
```


:::
:::


The adjusted Rand index (ARI) compares two partitions of the same people and is 0 for chance agreement
[@hubert1985comparing]. Changing only the scaling reassigns a large share of the patients.

### Step 4: a Gaussian mixture model


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc_z <- Mclust(x_z, G = 1:6, verbose = FALSE)
mc_log <- Mclust(x_logz, G = 1:6, verbose = FALSE)
c(z_scores = mc_z$G, log_z = mc_log$G)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> z_scores    log_z 
#>        6        3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(model_z = mc_z$modelName, model_log = mc_log$modelName)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   model_z model_log 
#>     "VVI"     "EEE"
```


:::
:::


### Step 5: bootstrap stability

For each resample, the persons are drawn with replacement, k-means is rerun, and every original cluster is compared
with its best-matching new cluster on the persons present in both (Jaccard similarity: shared persons divided by
persons in either). This follows the logic of Hennig's cluster-wise stability assessment; the same procedure is
available as `fpc::clusterboot()` [@hennig2007stability; @hennig2026fpc].


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bootstrap_stability <- function(x, k, n_boot = 100) {
  ref <- kmeans(x, centers = k, nstart = 25)$cluster
  jac <- matrix(NA_real_, n_boot, k)
  ari <- numeric(n_boot)
  for (b in seq_len(n_boot)) {
    idx <- sample(nrow(x), replace = TRUE)
    new <- kmeans(x[idx, ], centers = k, nstart = 10)$cluster
    present <- unique(idx)
    new_present <- new[match(present, idx)]       # new cluster of each person in the resample
    for (j in seq_len(k)) {
      a <- present[ref[present] == j]
      jac[b, j] <- max(sapply(seq_len(k), function(m) {
        bset <- present[new_present == m]
        length(intersect(a, bset)) / length(union(a, bset))
      }))
    }
    ari[b] <- adjustedRandIndex(ref[present], new_present)
  }
  list(jaccard = colMeans(jac), ari_median = median(ari))
}
set.seed(14142)
stab <- lapply(2:4, function(k) bootstrap_stability(x_z, k))
jac <- list(k2 = stab[[1]]$jaccard, k3 = stab[[2]]$jaccard, k4 = stab[[3]]$jaccard)
lapply(jac, round, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> $k2
#> [1] 0.95 0.94
#> 
#> $k3
#> [1] 0.91 0.77 0.82
#> 
#> $k4
#> [1] 0.89 0.96 0.84 0.72
```


:::
:::


### Step 6: look for a trough instead of a cluster count


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
valley_ratio_of <- function(x) {
  pc <- prcomp(x)$x[, 1]
  cl <- kmeans(x, centers = 2, nstart = 25)$cluster
  centres <- tapply(pc, cl, mean)
  dens <- density(pc, bw = "SJ")                  # kernel density of the first component
  f <- approxfun(dens$x, dens$y)
  f(mean(centres)) / mean(f(centres))             # density at the boundary / density at the centres
}
set.seed(14143)
valley_ratio <- valley_ratio_of(x_z)
round(valley_ratio, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 1.18
```


:::
:::


A ratio well below 1 points to a trough between two groups; a ratio near or above 1 means that the boundary runs
through a dense region. The ratio is a didactic diagnostic, not a formal test, and it looks only along the first
component.

### Step 7: the continuous baseline


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_cluster <- glm(organ_dysfunction ~ factor(cluster_ref), family = binomial)
fit_score <- glm(organ_dysfunction ~ pca$x[, 1], family = binomial)
aic_cluster <- AIC(fit_cluster)
aic_pc1 <- AIC(fit_score)
c(AIC_three_clusters = round(aic_cluster, 1), AIC_continuous_score = round(aic_pc1, 1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   AIC_three_clusters AIC_continuous_score 
#>                337.1                326.0
```


:::
:::


### Step 8: collect the variants and check the target values


::: {#tbl-b14-variants .cell tbl-cap='Results of the clustering variants on the same 300 synthetic persons. Silhouette: mean silhouette width; Jaccard: smallest mean bootstrap Jaccard similarity of the clusters (100 resamples); ARI: agreement with the reference solution (z-scores, k-means, k = 3).'}

```{.r .cell-code}
variants <- data.frame(
  Variant = c("z-scores, k-means, k = 2", "z-scores, k-means, k = 3 (reference)", "z-scores, k-means, k = 4",
              "original units, k-means, k = 3", "log + z-scores, k-means, k = 3",
              "z-scores, Gaussian mixture (BIC)", "log + z-scores, Gaussian mixture (BIC)"),
  Silhouette = c(cdsr_number(silhouette_mean[1:3], 2), "", "", "", ""),
  Jaccard = c(cdsr_number(sapply(jac, min), 2), "", "", "", ""),
  ARI = c("", "1.00", "", cdsr_number(ari_raw, 2), cdsr_number(ari_log, 2), "", ""),
  Components = c("2", "3", "4", "3", "3", as.character(mc_z$G), as.character(mc_log$G)))
knitr::kable(variants, align = "lrrrr")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Variant                                | Silhouette| Jaccard|  ARI| Components|
|:--------------------------------------|----------:|-------:|----:|----------:|
|z-scores, k-means, k = 2               |       0.34|    0.94|     |          2|
|z-scores, k-means, k = 3 (reference)   |       0.25|    0.77| 1.00|          3|
|z-scores, k-means, k = 4               |       0.23|    0.72|     |          4|
|original units, k-means, k = 3         |           |        | 0.37|          3|
|log + z-scores, k-means, k = 3         |           |        | 0.46|          3|
|z-scores, Gaussian mixture (BIC)       |           |        |     |          6|
|log + z-scores, Gaussian mixture (BIC) |           |        |     |          3|


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(
  pc1_share > 0.5, abs(cor_pc1) > 0.9,            # one dominant axis that tracks the hidden gradient
  mc_z$G > 1, mc_log$G > 1,                       # BIC prefers several components although there is no group
  min(jac$k3) > 0.75,                             # "stable" by the usual guidance ...
  valley_ratio > 0.8,                             # ... but no trough at the boundary
  ari_raw < 0.6,                                  # scaling changes the partition substantially
  aic_pc1 < aic_cluster                           # the continuous score is the better baseline
)
```
:::


### Step 9: an external test plan

A subtype hypothesis becomes testable when the analysis is frozen before new data are seen. @tbl-b14-plan lists a
minimal plan; each line names what would count against the hypothesis.

| Element | Fixed in advance | Counts against the subtype hypothesis |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline | markers, units, transformation, scaling, algorithm, k, seed, centres | any change after seeing the new cohort |
| Cohort | another centre or period, same assays and units, consecutive patients | selected or differently measured cohort |
| Reproduction | assign new patients to the frozen centres; recluster independently; compare (ARI, prediction strength [@tibshirani2005prediction]) | low agreement between frozen and new partition |
| Discontinuity | trough between clusters along the main axis | boundary in a dense region (ratio near or above 1) |
| Added value | clusters versus continuous score for a pre-specified outcome | no gain over the continuous score |
| Consequence | differential treatment effect in randomised data | effect identical across clusters |

: Minimal external test plan for a subtype hypothesis. {#tbl-b14-plan}

The last line is what the trial stratification would need. A published example of the kind of evidence it requires is
the latent class analysis of two randomised trials in acute respiratory distress syndrome, in which two
subphenotypes were found in both cohorts and the effect of the ventilation strategy differed by subphenotype in a
secondary analysis [@calfee2014subphenotypes]. Even there, the authors framed the result as useful for selecting
patients for future trials, not as a basis for treatment choice.

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python/umap-learn"}
The reference implementation of UMAP is the Python package umap-learn (version 0.5.12, April 2026;
[documentation](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)) [@mcinnes2018umap]. Its concrete advantage is direct
access to the original algorithm and its parameters (`n_neighbors`, `min_dist`, `metric`), which matters when a
published map is to be reproduced. For a fair comparison with an R workflow, the input matrix (same persons, same
transformation and scaling), the parameters, the random seed and the number of dimensions must be identical; even
then, different random initialisations can move islands. Status: conceptual comparison, not run. Any cluster seen on
such a map must pass the same checks as above on the original, unprojected data.
:::

**If the result stays unclear.** "No evidence for discrete subtypes; the markers vary along one continuous axis" is a
finding worth reporting. It comes with the continuous score, its distribution and the outcome model, which others can
test. When some diagnostics support groups and others do not, report all of them and keep the language at
"candidate clusters" until the external plan has been run.

## Counter-check {#sec-b14-countercheck}

Change the data, not the method: generate the same six markers from a severity score with a real gap – two groups of
150 people centred at −1.2 and +1.2 with a within-group spread of 0.45 (*assumption*). **Predict first:** which of the
diagnostics will change markedly – the BIC component count, the bootstrap Jaccard similarity, the silhouette width or
the trough ratio?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1415)
severity_gap <- c(rnorm(n / 2, -1.2, 0.45), rnorm(n / 2, 1.2, 0.45))
x_gap <- scale(make_markers(severity_gap))
km_gap <- kmeans(x_gap, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
km_grad2 <- km[[1]]
compare <- data.frame(
  Diagnostic = c("mean silhouette, k = 2", "smallest bootstrap Jaccard, k = 2", "trough ratio",
                 "Gaussian mixture components (BIC)"),
  Gradient = c(silhouette_mean[["k=2"]], min(jac$k2), valley_ratio, mc_z$G),
  Gap = c(mean(silhouette(km_gap$cluster, dist(x_gap))[, "sil_width"]),
          min(bootstrap_stability(x_gap, 2)$jaccard),
          valley_ratio_of(x_gap),
          Mclust(x_gap, G = 1:6, verbose = FALSE)$G))
compare$Gradient <- round(compare$Gradient, 2); compare$Gap <- round(compare$Gap, 2)
compare
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                          Diagnostic Gradient  Gap
#> 1            mean silhouette, k = 2     0.34 0.49
#> 2 smallest bootstrap Jaccard, k = 2     0.94 0.99
#> 3                      trough ratio     1.18 0.35
#> 4 Gaussian mixture components (BIC)     6.00 4.00
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(compare$Gap[3] < 0.5, compare$Gradient[3] > 0.8,       # the trough separates the two situations
          compare$Gap[1] > compare$Gradient[1],                    # silhouette rises, but modestly
          abs(compare$Gap[2] - compare$Gradient[2]) < 0.1)         # stability hardly differs
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
boundary_of <- function(x, cl) mean(tapply(prcomp(x)$x[, 1], cl, mean))
hist_df <- rbind(data.frame(scenario = "Gradient (no groups)", pc1 = prcomp(x_z)$x[, 1]),
                 data.frame(scenario = "Two groups with a gap", pc1 = prcomp(x_gap)$x[, 1]))
bounds <- data.frame(scenario = c("Gradient (no groups)", "Two groups with a gap"),
                     b = c(boundary_of(x_z, km_grad2$cluster), boundary_of(x_gap, km_gap$cluster)))
ggplot(hist_df, aes(pc1)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = cdsr_colours[["skyblue"]], colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(data = bounds, aes(xintercept = b), colour = cdsr_colours[["red"]], linetype = cdsr_linetypes[[2]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ scenario) +
  labs(x = "PC1 (z-scored markers)", y = "Persons") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![First principal component of z-scored markers for a continuous gradient and for two groups with a real gap (*synthetic*, n = 300 persons each). Vertical line: boundary between the two k-means clusters.](b14-cluster-gradient-artefact_files/figure-epub/fig-b14-countercheck-1.png){#fig-b14-countercheck fig-alt='Two histograms side by side. On the left, the gradient: one broad peak with the k-means boundary near its centre. On the right, the gap scenario: two peaks separated by a trough, with the boundary in the trough.'}
:::
:::


The trough ratio falls from 1.18 to 0.35, and the silhouette width rises from
0.34 to 0.49. Bootstrap stability hardly changes (0.94 versus
0.99): it was already high for the gradient. The mixture model selects 4 components for
two groups, which again shows that the BIC count describes the shape of the density, not the number of patient groups.
Only the diagnostics that look for empty space between groups separate the two situations.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b14-consequences}

**Patients and ethics.** A subtype label travels. It enters records, referral letters and conversations, and it can
change expectations about recovery. A person labelled "hyperinflammatory" because their values lie just across an
arbitrary boundary may receive a different treatment from a neighbour with almost identical values. A subtype name
therefore needs a justified consequence: a treatment, monitoring or prognosis decision that differs by subtype and has
been shown to do so, as in the external plan above. Without it, the continuous score is more honest and loses less
information. If the markers differ systematically by sex, age or laboratory method, clusters can become proxies for
these characteristics; check the distribution of such variables across clusters before naming them (@sec-b21).

**Regulation.** Exploratory clustering in a research data set is not a medical device. If software assigned patients
to subtypes in order to select a treatment, its intended purpose would have to be assessed under the medical device
rules (@sec-b22).

**Data protection and security.** A cluster label derived from personal data is itself personal data. Small clusters
with unusual marker combinations can make individuals recognisable in published figures or supplementary tables
(@sec-b23). Security is only indirectly relevant: the frozen pipeline of the external plan, including centres and
seed, must be stored and versioned so that the test cannot be adjusted after the fact.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b14-lookup}

**Reviewer question.** Did the authors show a gap between clusters that survives a change of scaling and reappears in
an independent cohort, and does the cluster label predict the outcome better than a continuous score?

**Self-test.** A manuscript reports four "immune subtypes" after polytrauma, found with k-means on z-scored markers.
The authors cite mean bootstrap Jaccard similarities above 0.85 and a BIC-selected mixture model with four components
as validation. What is missing?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both arguments are compatible with a continuous gradient: k-means cuts a gradient reproducibly, and BIC adds
components to describe a skewed or curved density. Missing are evidence of a discontinuity (a trough or clear
separation that survives other scalings and algorithms), reproduction in an independent cohort with a frozen
pipeline, and a comparison with a continuous score. A treatment consequence would additionally need a differential
effect in randomised data.
:::

**Annotated sources.**

- @hennig2007stability – cluster-wise bootstrap stability with the Jaccard similarity; the method behind Step 5.
- @hennig2026fpc – documentation of `clusterboot()`, including the usual interpretation thresholds for the mean
  Jaccard similarity.
- @scrucca2016mclust – the Gaussian mixture models and BIC-based model choice used in Step 4.
- @hartigan1979kmeans – the k-means algorithm that R's `kmeans()` uses by default.
- @rousseeuw1987silhouette and @hubert1985comparing – silhouette width and adjusted Rand index.
- @tibshirani2005prediction – prediction strength as a check of whether clusters reproduce in new data.
- @mcinnes2018umap, @umaplearn2026docs and @chari2023specious – how UMAP works, the warning about false tears, and how
  far two-dimensional embeddings can distort structure.
- @calfee2014subphenotypes – a published subphenotype analysis that tested reproduction in two cohorts and a
  differential treatment effect.
